newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe government withdraws farm levies bill.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe government withdraws farm levies bill.

text.p: The Zimbabwe government on Tuesday withdrew a bill imposing levies on agriculture following strong objections from commercial farmers who said it threatened their viability.

The bill was presented to parliament earlier in the day, but Agriculture Minister Denis Norman said he was temporarily withdrawing it to allow consultations with farming leaders who said they had been taken by surprise by its introduction.
"I wish to withdraw the bill to enable further consultation and consideration to take place...I will re-present the bill to parliament in the new year," he said, without elaborating.
Farming leaders said the bill would harm their sector, a mainstay of the economy. But Tobias Takavarasha, permanent secretary in the ministry of agriculture, said it would enhance development.

The Agricultural Products Marketing Bill would impose levies on at least 27 products, mostly food, including the country's staple maize and some crops rarely grown in the southern African state, such as black-eyed peas.
The bill said the levies would be set by a board appointed by the agriculture minister and would be used to fund research, marketing and provision of technical and advisory services.

But many farming leaders said they doubted the motives behind the bill and were lobbying for rejection by members of President Robert Mugabe's ruling ZANU-PF party which holds 147 of the 150 seats in parliament.

"Corporate tax is already too high without new levies...no matter what you call them, and the bottom line of what we are facing is that it is going to affect producers' viability," said David Hasluck, director of the main and predominantly white Commercial Farmers Union (CFU).
"We were not consulted on this surprising bill and I think we need to discuss the issue further with the government," he told Reuters.

David Zhou, the deputy director of the mainly black Zimbabwe Farmers Union (ZFU), said producers would carry the burden of the new levies although the government proposes that they should be split between producers, buyers, processors and marketeers.
"Experience elsewhere shows everybody passes back the cost to the producer and I don't see how this will be different. The farmer is simply looking at double taxation here," he added.

The Indigenous (black) Commercial Farmers Union (ICFU), a pressure group fighting for economic empowerment of Zimbabwe's black majority, had welcomed the proposed levies, saying the government should use the taxes to develop agricultural infrastructure, such as dams and roads, in disadvantaged districts.
"That's the way forward," said ICFU president Thomas Nherera.

Earlier this year, Zimbabwe's cash-strapped government -- struggling to balance its books and under pressure to cut its spending which currently accounts for about 40 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) -- introduced a 10 percent levy on tobacco despite strong opposition from farmers.
